title: 工会状态：游戏行业工会化的兴起
content:
State of the Unions: the rise of unionisation in games workplaces | GamesIndustry.biz

The rise of unions in the video games industry has been a hot topic over the past decade, as more and more workers seek protection for their rights in the face of harsh working conditions and management shortcomings around the world.
Not only have a large number of games-specific unions formed in a relatively short amount of time, but these unions have already demonstrated their value for members. SAG-AFTRA went on strike to secure improved pay and AI protections for video games voice actors, ZeniMax workers have marched out over
disagreements around remote work and outsourcing
, and union-organised protests have been held outside the premises of Rockstar Games, Activision, Ubisoft, Bethesda, Riot Games, and Build A Rocket Boy (to name but a few).
It's a trend that shows every sign of continuing, and working successfully with unions has become increasingly important in games workplaces – in fact, we'll be discussing this topic deeper at
our upcoming HR Summit on October 1
. It reflects a new reality in the industry, after years in which union discussions were all but non-existent.
Austin Kelmore |
Image credit:
Austin Kelmore
"When Game Workers Unite launched eight years ago, there were hardly any unions or game workers in unions," says Austin Kelmore, co-founder of the IWGB Game Workers and Game Worker Solidarity. "Since then, workers in more than 130 distinct groups and unions in over 15 countries have organized together to win real improvements in their workplaces. The conversation has shifted from 'Should the games industry unionize?' to 'Which workers are going to unionize next?'
"We are making our voices heard and winning big in the process. We still have a long way to go to fully unionize the games industry, but we've made an incredible amount of progress in a relatively small amount of time."
Marc Rutschlé, one of the union representatives of Solidaires Informatique at Ubisoft Paris, adds: "At Ubisoft, unions have largely progressed in the French studios. Five years ago, there were no unions inside the 'Comité Social et Economique' (the workers councils). Right now, unions are present in almost every Ubisoft company in France and some structures have several unions. This is pretty standard for a French company. It basically means the social dialogue at Ubisoft is becoming mature.
IWGB lead protests outside Build A Rocket Boy following layoffs earlier this year. |
Image credit:
IWGB Game Workers Union
"Unfortunately, the rest of the French video games industry is completely collapsing. Almost every major studio has fallen into bankruptcy or is starting layoff plans. It's hard to say what will happen in just one to two years."
The Polish Gamedev Workers Union was formed just two years ago as part of a nationwide grassroots trade union, The Workers Initiative. Union member Artur Ganszyniec reports the organisation is officially established within ten Polish studios, which accounts for just half of its members, the rest working for various smaller companies.
"One of our main challenges is the legal framework governing trade unions in Poland – most of the laws were written in the '80s and with heavy industry in mind, and they do not represent the realities of creative or remote work," Ganszyniec explains. "The law is also written in favour of the employers, severely limiting the role of the unions."
Artur Ganszyniec |
Image credit:
Artur Ganszyniec
Nonetheless, the Polish Gamedev Workers Union has already been able to represent employees during layoffs, offered legal aid, helped people navigate the complexities of Polish labor law, negotiated workplace regulations, and offered an informal support network for members.
These are just some examples of what unions have been able to accomplish. Kelmore adds that workers in games unions around the world have managed to secure four-day work weeks, pay increases, hybrid and remote working arrangements, AI protections, contractual bonuses, six-hour work days, and more. Unions have also helped reduce the number of people laid off, stopped harassment, and won millions of dollars for mistreated workers.
"My own boss tried to discipline me and I was able to successfully get it dismissed," Kelmore adds. "I have worked with coworkers to secure better redundancy terms for those affected and those who stayed behind.
"In addition to working and material conditions, workers in unions have learned they have the power to collectively effect change in their workplaces and the world at large. It may sound cheesy, but once people experience for themselves the process of creating change, they will never forget it. That will help them push for change inside and outside of the workplace."
More importantly, unions have not only been able to change the lives of the staff they represent, but also had a significant impact on the companies they're negotiating with.
"Early on, a large portion of our casework was teaching people who ran companies what the law is and forcing them to follow it," says Kelmore. "This meant companies had to learn how to properly follow disciplinary, grievance, and redundancy procedures. They had to accommodate disabilities and neurodiverse staff in the ways that are legally mandated. They had to learn the workers know more about the law than they do and the workers were willing to enforce it.
The IWGB has steadily increased its profile in the UK. |
Image credit:
IWGB Game Workers Union
"As unions become larger and workers have built more power, we've been able to apply pressure to those at the top and improve things in two ways: advocate and push for the things we want and stop harmful treatment from those who employ us.
